channel.title: Darrell Holliday, writing
channel.description: Notes on offers, sales conversations, and using AI once something is already selling.

item.title: Don’t build a funnel until someone has actually bought
item.description: A landing page and email sequence will not fix an offer nobody has said yes to. Get a sale by hand first, then build the path around it.
item.content:encoded:
I hear a version of this every week. “I’m building the funnel first, then I’ll start talking to people.”

The landing page is almost done. The email sequence is mapped. The booking calendar is connected to a tool they set up at 1 a.m. And they have not asked a single person to buy.

A funnel is a way to repeat a sale you already understand. If you do not yet know why someone would say yes, you are decorating a guess.

Here’s the order I use, and the one I ask clients to use.

Write the offer in plain words. Who it’s for, what changes, why now, and what you want them to do next. If you cannot say that in a short paragraph, you are not ready for a page, let alone a six-step sequence.

Make a short list of people you can already reach. Not “my audience.” Names. People who have already talked to you, already asked a question, or already work in the world you want to serve.

Talk to them. A call, a voice note, a direct message that is actually a conversation. Tell them who the offer is for and what it does. Ask if they want to do it. When they hesitate, write down the hesitation. That sentence is more useful than any headline generator.

Get a yes, or a clear no, before you build the machine. A yes tells you what to keep. A no tells you what to fix. A silent landing page tells you nothing.

Then, and only then, build the smallest path that would have made that sale easier: a simple page, a follow-up message you can reuse, a way to book the next call. That is a funnel. It is just the conversation you already had, written down.

I’ve watched people spend months on tools and pages for an offer nobody had agreed to pay for. I’ve also watched first sales happen from a Google Doc and a calendar link, because the offer was clear and the person asked.

If you have been “finishing the funnel” for three weeks, stop this week. Pick five people. Have the conversation. Build the funnel around what you learn, not around what you hope.

item.title: Have these conversations before you add another AI tool
item.description: A short list, a clear ask, and a follow-up. That’s the work that has to happen before you automate anything.
item.content:encoded:
If your week is full of new tools and empty of conversations, the business is not being built. The stack is.

I like AI. I use it. I also don’t start there with a client who isn’t selling yet. Sales still come from a person hearing an offer and deciding to buy. The tools can wait a week.

Here are the conversations I want you to have before you add another AI tool.

The offer conversation, with yourself. Out loud, not in a doc you keep rewriting. Who is this for? What changes for them? Why would they do it this month? What’s the next step? If any of those answers are fuzzy, that’s the job. Not a new model.

The five-name conversation. Write down five people you can already reach who might be the buyer, or who know the buyer. If you cannot name five, your offer is probably aimed at “people online,” which is not a market. Tighten it until names appear.

The direct ask. Message or call those five and say what you’re offering, in plain words, and ask if they want to talk about it. Not “I’ve been working on something, would love your feedback.” That’s a way to hide. Ask.

The debrief. After each conversation, write down what they repeated, where they hesitated, and what they asked next. Those are the words that belong in the offer. They are better than anything a prompt will invent.

The follow-up. Most first conversations do not end in a yes. The sale, when it happens, is often in the second or third message, the one most people never send. Write that follow-up yourself, once. You can let AI draft the next ones after you know what a good one sounds like.

That’s a week of work. It does not require a new subscription. When you’ve had those conversations, you’ll know what to automate: the follow-up you were already willing to send, the outline you already believe, the notes you already take. Until then, another tool is a way to avoid the part that feels like rejection.

Do the conversations this week. Add the tool after you have something worth repeating.

item.title: What to automate after your first sales, and what to leave alone
item.description: Once an offer is selling, automate follow-up, drafts, and the weekly routine. Leave the buying conversation with you.
item.content:encoded:
The right time to automate is after you can explain, in plain words, how a sale actually happened.

Not after you bought a course on automations. After a person has paid you, and you can say what they needed to hear, how they found you, and what you did next. Then you have something worth repeating.

Here’s what I tell people to automate first.

Follow-up. The messages you already send after a call, or after someone goes quiet. Write one good version. Let AI draft the later ones, in your words, for you to send. Do not let a bot start a conversation you would not start.

Drafts, not decisions. Outlines for a post, a first pass at an onboarding email, a summary of the notes from a call. You still cut the fluff and hit send. That’s how you get the time back without handing over the relationship.

A weekly routine you can keep. A reminder to run your short list. A checklist for the week’s conversations. A simple place to record what happened. This is boring, and it’s the difference between a good month and a disappearing act in week three.

Here’s what I tell people to leave alone, even after the first sales.

The first real conversation with a buyer. Don’t outsource the ask, the discovery, or the close to a chatbot because you’re tired of hearing no. That’s the work that teaches you what the offer actually is.

Anything you cannot yet explain. If the only reason you’re automating a step is “I think this is what a proper business does,” you’re building someone else’s diagram. Wait until you have done the step by hand often enough to know what “good” looks like.

A complicated lead machine for a tiny offer. If you are still selling to people you can already reach, you do not need a 12-step nurture system. You need a clear offer, a calendar, and follow-up.

I use AI every week, and I still read what it writes before a buyer does. The clients who get leverage from it are the ones who automated a process they could already run, not the ones who hoped the tools would invent the process.

If you have a few sales and you’re itching to “systemize,” start with follow-up, drafts, and a weekly routine. Leave the conversation with you. That’s the part people are paying for.

item.title: Treat your AI tools like interns, not employees
item.description: AI is fast and cheap and it will confidently do the wrong thing. Here’s the standard I hold it to.
item.content:encoded:
I like AI. I use it every week. I also don’t let it talk to a buyer until I’ve read what it wrote.

The simplest way to think about it: your AI tools are interns.

Interns are useful. They draft, they research, they organize. They also invent details, miss the point, and will hit send if you let them. You wouldn’t put an intern on a sales call alone in week one. Don’t do that with a chatbot either.

Here’s the standard I use with clients.

Interns draft. You decide. Let it write the first version of the offer, the follow-up, the outline. Then you cut the fluff and fix anything you wouldn’t say out loud.

Interns need a tight brief. \"Write my sales page\" is how you get sludge. \"Here’s who it’s for, here’s the before and after, don’t use these words\" is how you get something you can edit.

Interns don’t own the relationship. If a person is waiting on a reply, you send it. Automation can remind you. It shouldn’t pretend to be you.

Fire the intern from any job that’s failing. If the output is consistently off, the prompt is wrong, or the job shouldn’t be automated yet. Go back to doing it by hand for a week. You’ll learn more than you will by adding another tool.

The people who make money with AI aren’t the ones with the biggest stack. They’re the ones who kept a human in the loop, especially where trust is the product.

Use the intern. Don’t give it the keys.

item.title: What 12 weeks of one-on-one coaching actually looks like
item.description: No mystery container. Here’s the work, week by week, and what I expect from you.
item.content:encoded:
People ask what coaching with me actually is. Fair question. \"12 weeks of 1:1\" can mean anything.

Here’s what it means when you work with me.

Week 1. We get specific. Who the offer is for, what changes for them, and what \"this worked\" looks like in 90 days, as a number. If we can’t say those things in plain words, we don’t build anything else yet.

Weeks 2 to 6. You talk to people. Not a thousand strangers. A short list, conversations with people you can already reach, a clear next step. I help you prep, debrief, and fix the offer when someone’s face tells us it’s off. The goal is first sales, or a clear reason why they said no.

Weeks 7 to 12. Only then do we build systems. Follow-up, simple AI drafts, a weekly routine you can keep when I’m not on the call. We automate what’s already working. We don’t build a machine for an offer nobody has bought.

Between calls. You can message me with a quick question. I won’t run your business for you, and I won’t need a 40-page update. Send the thing you’re stuck on.

What I expect from you. Show up. Do the conversations. Tell me the truth when something flopped. This fails when someone wants a plan more than they want to talk to buyers.

What I won’t promise. A specific income number. Anyone who does is guessing, or selling you a story.

If that sounds like the kind of help you want, apply. We’ll see if it’s a fit.

item.title: Most people quit in week three. Here’s how I coach them through it.
item.description: The excitement is gone, the results aren’t here yet, and that’s exactly when the business gets built.
item.content:encoded:
Week one is exciting. New plan, new tools, big energy.

Week two is busy. Lots of setup. It still feels like progress.

Week three is where people disappear.

The novelty is gone. The first post got four likes. The first sales conversation went nowhere. Life shows up. And the little voice says \"maybe this isn’t for me.\"

I’ve seen this pattern often. Here’s what I do about it.

I tell them it’s coming. On day one. \"Around week three, this is going to feel pointless. That’s normal. That’s the part where most people quit, and it’s the part where the business actually gets built.\" When it hits, they recognize it instead of believing it.

I shrink the goal. Nobody needs a 12-step plan in week three. They need one thing to finish this week. One offer page. Five conversations. One post. Small enough that they can’t talk themselves out of it.

I go back to why they started. Not in a fluffy way. I ask what life looks like in six months if this works, and what it looks like if they stop now. That used to be a sales technique for me. Now it’s how I keep people from quitting on themselves.

I look for proof, not perfection. Did someone reply? Did anyone ask a question? Did they get a \"not now\" instead of silence? That’s movement. I point it out, because they usually won’t.

Coaching isn’t about having better information than the internet. The information is free. Coaching is about getting someone through the boring middle, where most people stop.

If you’re in week three of something right now, keep going. Shrink the goal. Finish one thing this week.

item.title: Your first $1,000 online is an offer problem, not a traffic problem
item.description: Most new businesses think they need more people. They usually need a clearer reason for the first 10 to buy.
item.content:encoded:
When someone tells me they need more traffic, I ask one question.

\"If 10 of the right people saw your offer today, how many would buy?\"

Usually there’s a long pause. Then: \"I don’t know.\"

That’s the problem. Not traffic.

When you’re starting out, you don’t need thousands of visitors. You need a small number of people who read your offer and think \"that’s exactly me.\" If you can’t get that reaction from 10 people you know, 10,000 strangers won’t fix it.

Here’s what I look at first with a new business:

Who exactly is it for? \"Entrepreneurs\" is not an answer. \"Fitness coaches who sell 1:1 and want a group program\" is an answer.

What changes for them? Not features. The before and after, in their words.

Why now? What makes this worth paying for this month instead of someday?

Why you? One honest reason. A result, a story, a skill. It doesn’t have to be huge. It has to be true.

What’s the next step? One. Apply, buy the thing, or join the list. Not three options.

Get those five right and your first sales usually come from people you can already reach: your network, your DMs, a few honest posts about what you’re building.

Then you earn the right to worry about traffic.

I’ve watched people spend months on ads and funnels for an offer nobody had said yes to yet. I’ve also watched people make their first few thousand dollars with a Google Doc and a calendar link. The second group had a clear offer.

Start there.

item.title: AI won’t sell your offer for you
item.description: AI makes the work faster. It doesn’t make anyone want what you’re selling. Here’s where it actually helps.
item.content:encoded:
Every week I talk to someone who has built an impressive AI setup and made zero dollars.

They have the custom GPT. The automated content calendar. The landing page that took 40 minutes instead of four days. And no sales.

I get it. Building feels like progress. Selling feels like rejection.

But here’s the truth I learned from years of sales calls: people don’t buy because your process is efficient. They buy because you understand their problem better than they do, and they believe you can get them out of it.

AI can’t fake that for you. It can help you get there faster.

Here’s where I tell people to use it.

Research before you build. Use AI to pull apart the language your buyers use. Reviews, forum threads, comments. You’re looking for the exact words people use to describe the problem. Those words go in your offer.

Draft, then talk. Let AI write the first version of your offer. Then get on calls with five people and watch where their face changes. Rewrite based on that, not on the prompt.

Follow-up, not first touch. The money is in the follow-up. AI is great at drafting the second, third and fourth message you were never going to send. You still decide what goes out.

Delivery, once you have buyers. Templates, onboarding docs, checklists. This is where AI saves you hours, because now you know what people actually need.

Notice the order. Sell first. Automate what’s working.

If your AI stack is bigger than your customer list, flip your week around. Spend the next five days talking to buyers. The tools will still be there.

item.title: I sold about $12M over Zoom. Then I stopped selling and started coaching.
item.description: Why I walked away from the close, and why the same skills turned out to matter more after the sale.
item.content:encoded:
For years my job was the close.

Software. Education. Coaching programs from $5K to $50K. Somewhere around $12M in lifetime sales, most of it on Zoom calls with people who were scared to spend the money and more scared to stay where they were.

I was good at it. I also built the funnels, the offers, the pricing and the follow-up emails. If you’ve ever bought a high-ticket program online, there’s a decent chance someone like me was on the other end of that call.

And then I burned out.

Not dramatically. I just noticed I felt empty after a big week. The number went up and I didn’t care. I kept thinking about the people I’d enrolled. Did they actually do the thing? Did it work? I had no idea. My job ended when they paid.

So I moved to the other side of the table. I started coaching.

Here’s what surprised me. Every skill I learned closing works even better after the sale.

Tie-downs become commitments. \"So if we get this done by Friday, you’re ready to launch, right?\"

Future pacing becomes the reason people keep going in week three, when the excitement is gone and the work is boring.

Reframes are how you talk someone off the ledge when their first launch makes $0.

The difference is who it’s for. On a sales call, those tools serve the company. In coaching, they serve the person in front of you.

I’ve now coached 350+ people building online businesses, most of them using AI to do it. The ones who get paid aren’t the ones with the best tools. They’re the ones who sell something specific, to someone specific, and keep showing up when the excitement fades.

That’s what I help with now. Sales is where my credibility comes from. Coaching is the work I actually want to do.

If you’re building something online and you’re stuck between \"I’ve learned a lot\" and \"I’ve made money,\" that gap is my favorite place to work.
